hops.title: The rattlesnake tail that never fuses into tetanus
hops.text: A western diamondback rattlesnake can shake its tail for hours at close to ninety cycles a second. Drive one of your calf's motor units that fast and its twitches would blend into steady force. A rattle needs a separate pulse of force on every shake. The snake's shaker muscles, like the toadfish swimbladder muscles behind its two-hundred-hertz boatwhistle call, keep every twitch separate: calcium is released and cleared very fast, and the force-making proteins let go quickly. About a quarter of each shaker fibre's volume is calcium-storing membrane, and another quarter is mitochondria. Electrical recordings suggest each of the snake's six shaker muscles may be a single motor unit.

sources.citation: Schaeffer, Conley & Lindstedt, J. Exp. Biol. 199(Pt 2):351-358 (1996)
Rome et al., Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 93(15):8095-8100 (1996)

image.caption: Rattlesnake shaker muscles deliver a separate force pulse nearly ninety times a second, for hours.

hops.title: The Pinocchio illusion: vibrating a tendon to grow a nose
hops.text: In 1972, physiologists vibrated volunteers' biceps or triceps tendons at one hundred hertz. While the muscle was contracting, people misjudged their elbow angle by up to forty degrees, feeling the joint as if the vibrated muscle had been stretched. The vibration drives the spindle endings directly, mimicking stretch. In 1988, James Lackner showed it can also distort perceived body shape. Close your eyes, hold the tip of your nose, and have the biceps tendon vibrated: the spindles report an arm straightening and a hand moving away, while the fingertip still feels the nose. In some people, the brain reconciles the two by deciding the nose is growing.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student with closed eyes sits in a chair holding the tip of their nose while a small handheld vibration device rests against the inside of their bent elbow.
image.caption: Vibrating the biceps tendon fakes a spindle stretch signal, so a held nose can feel as if it grows.

hops.title: Newborn stepping that was never switched off
hops.text: A newborn held upright with the feet on a table marches in an alternating rhythm. By about two months this stepping usually fades, and it was widely believed that the maturing cortex had switched off a primitive reflex. Esther Thelen and her colleagues tested a plainer explanation: heavy legs. Lying on their backs, babies keep making the same kicking movement for months. In four-week-old infants, small weights strapped to the legs cut stepping by about a third, and lowering the legs into a tank of warm water nearly doubled it. As the authors pointed out, water should not release cortical inhibition.

sources.citation: Thelen, Fisher & Ridley-Johnson, Infant Behav. Dev. 7(4):479-493 (1984)
Thelen, Fisher, Ridley-Johnson & Griffin, Dev. Psychobiol. 15(5):447-453 (1982)
Adolph & Franchak, Wiley Interdiscip. Rev. Cogn. Sci. 8(1-2):e1430 (2017)

image.caption: Buoyed by warm water, four-week-old infants nearly doubled their stepping; small leg weights cut it by a third.
